bridges.mechanism: A sudden drop in crude supply reframes energy shortfalls as national-security emergencies, prompting governments to fast-track rulemaking, export controls and oversight of dual‑use technologies (including AI) to protect critical infrastructure and manage risks.

A sudden drop in crude supply from the Middle East raises headline inflation and inflation expectations through higher transport and energy costs, prompting central banks to raise policy rates to defend inflation targets.

Reduced crude availability increases expected future inflation and term premia, pushing up nominal yields across maturities and steepening/raising the yield curve as investors demand compensation for higher expected inflation and risk.

A substantive drop in available crude from the Middle East increases buyers' dependence on alternative exporters (notably Russia) and strengthens those suppliers' diplomatic leverage, prompting importing governments to dial back the severity or scope of sanctions to secure uninterrupted supplies.

Sharp and unpredictable swings in energy prices increase operational and financing risk for energy‑intensive AI data centers and training projects, causing investors and firms to pull or delay new capital allocations into advanced AI capacity.

High and volatile energy prices raise domestic economic and political costs for energy‑importing governments, making them less willing to sustain or escalate multilateral sanctions on Russia to avoid further price shocks at home.

Sharp, persistent swings in oil and gas prices elevate market risk premia and policymaker concern about resource-driven competition, directly raising perceived geopolitical risk between major powers including the US and China.

Rising attacks and losses in key sea lanes prompt navies and private maritime operators to field AI-driven surveillance, autonomy and counter-drone systems, accelerating the operational deployment rate of models for maritime tasks.

Escalating threats to vessels in key chokepoints raises insurance and security costs and forces some traders and banks to suspend or curtail payments and lending tied to affected routes, reducing the net rate of cross-border trade and associated capital flows.

Rising maritime threats in Middle Eastern chokepoints force allied navies, airlift and escort resources to be reassigned to protect commercial traffic and regional partners, reducing the available lift, convoy protection and logistics throughput for weapons and equipment deliveries to Ukraine.

An increase in attacks or perceived risk in key sea lanes raises insurance and transport costs and prompts investors to delay or redirect FDI in export-oriented and import-dependent projects, reducing cross-border investment flows between blocs (including US↔China) within investment decision cycles.

Tighter sanctions enforcement blocks exports of high-end accelerators, cloud services and specialized software to targeted actors, directly reducing their capacity to train large models and thus slowing local model development velocity.

Tighter, actively enforced sanctions disrupt correspondent banking relationships and close payment corridors for targeted jurisdictions and counterparties, directly reducing bank and portfolio capital flows into and out of those jurisdictions.

Tighter and more aggressive enforcement of sanctions and interdictions in the Middle East raises inspection, seizure and insurance risks for energy shipments, prompting route cancellations, transshipment delays and carrier avoidance that directly disrupt cross‑border energy supply continuity.

Tighter, more rigorously enforced sanctions on shipping, finance and intermediary suppliers restrict deliveries of specialized equipment and financing for fab projects, causing delays, cancellations or reduced throughput of advanced semiconductor fabs.

A sustained rise in the pace of rerouting shipments away from Middle East chokepoints forces firms to source from additional geographies and build alternative logistics nodes, directly increasing the geographic spread of suppliers and production nodes.

An increase in coercive_escalation (more intense cross‑border kinetic, paramilitary or hybrid operations) elevates geopolitical risk and term premiums, pushing up nominal sovereign yields across maturities as investors price higher risk and potential economic disruption.

Increased kinetic and hybrid operations tied to the Russia‑Ukraine war (attacks on ports, mine‑laying, naval skirmishes, or proxy strikes) raises observable risks to vessels and crews in adjacent sea lanes and can spill over into chokepoints used by Middle Eastern energy shipping.

Spikes in cross‑border kinetic and hybrid attacks create immediate market and policymaker fear of conflict spillover and supply disruption, raising perceived geopolitical risk relevant to US–China trade and investment decisions.

Targeted export controls and financial restrictions cut off access to specialized chips, cloud compute and cross-border collaboration, directly delaying training runs and slowing iteration on new model architectures.

An increase in sanction_pressure (coordinated asset freezes, transaction bans and trade restrictions) directly restricts targeted entities' access to the international banking and payments system, reducing net cross‑border capital flows as funds are frozen, blocked or rerouted.

Expansion or tightening of multilateral sanctions and secondary‑sanctions risk around Russian oil exports directly removes barrels from accessible global markets and deters buyers, reducing aggregate crude availability for immediate trade.

Widespread and sustained sanctions regimes against Russia normalize stricter licensing, expanded control lists and enforcement capacity, prompting governments to tighten export controls on sensitive technologies that could flow to China.

Large, rapid deliveries of military hardware and funded capability packages include turnkey AI-enabled sensors, autonomy modules, and integration contracts that directly accelerate fielding of trained models into operational systems.

An increase in defense_aid_flow (higher volumes of military equipment transfers and government procurement) raises immediate cross‑border financial transactions and trade financing, mechanically increasing net cross‑border capital flow rates.

Higher political and operational alignment among allied states enables coordinated rulemaking (export controls, procurement standards, certification regimes) that raises regulatory and compliance expectations for AI developers.

Stronger political and operational alignment among allies in response to the Russia‑Ukraine war produces coordinated legal measures, information‑sharing and joint interdiction efforts that increase the operational rigor of sanctions enforcement affecting energy flows.

Greater political and operational alignment among Western allies over the Ukraine response leads to coordinated investment‑screening and political pressure that reduces Chinese FDI and other cross‑border investments into allied markets.

Interruptions or price spikes in cross‑border energy supplies force data centers and research facilities to curtail high‑intensity training workloads or postpone experiments, directly reducing the pace of model development.

An increase in energy_flow_stability (more reliable cross‑border energy supplies) reduces headline energy-driven inflation and the upside shock to consumer prices, lowering the near‑term need for central banks to raise policy interest rates.

Interruptions or volatility in cross‑border energy infrastructure (e.g., pipeline closures, damaged export terminals, or constrained shipping from Black Sea corridors) force traders and tankers to divert cargoes to alternative routes, ports or suppliers at an accelerated pace.

Disruptions and volatility in energy supplies force firms to relocate or source energy‑intensive production and inputs from a wider set of countries, increasing geographic diversification of supply chains.

Increases in advanced domestic semiconductor fabrication capacity raise the supply and lower the cost of accelerators and custom chips, directly enabling larger-scale training runs and faster model iteration.

A meaningful increase in advanced chip fabrication capacity eases semiconductor supply constraints, reducing projected goods-price pressures and precautionary term premia, which exerts downward pressure on longer-maturity nominal yields.

An increase in allied/domestic advanced semiconductor fabrication capacity raises available supplies of critical components for precision munitions, drones and targeting systems, enabling higher and more sustained transfers of those systems to Ukraine and its partners.

Greater geographic diversification of critical supply chains lowers concentration and earnings-volatility risk for corporates, reducing equity risk premia and prompting institutional investors to tilt portfolios toward equities and away from safe cash/bond holdings.

Corporate moves to diversify supply chains away from China create new production and transshipment points, which directly increases the rate at which energy and goods shipments are re-routed to alternative sea lanes, hubs and logistics corridors.

When Western governments and firms materially diversify supply chains away from China, the reduced economic exposure lowers political risk of Chinese retaliation and makes governments more willing to impose or tighten coordinated trade and financial sanctions on Russia.

Higher cross-border investment flows inject direct equity, M&A proceeds, and venture funding into foreign AI firms and labs, immediately increasing the net rate of financial resources available for advanced AI development.

Stricter export controls block or delay shipment of high-end AI accelerators, pre-trained models, and cloud services to targeted firms, directly reducing available training throughput and slowing iteration cycles.

Tightening export controls immediately blocks transactions and raises compliance/legal risk, prompting foreign investors, banks and trading partners to pause or withdraw capital and trade finance to affected firms and jurisdictions, reducing net cross-border capital flows.

Tighter export controls on critical technologies to China prompt Beijing to accelerate spot purchases and build strategic reserves of Middle East crude to hedge against supply-chain pressure, drawing down volumes available to third‑party buyers.

Tighter export controls on advanced technologies toward China require and incentivize multilateral coordination (sharing rules, enforcement, intelligence), which increases political and operational alignment among US partners and allies on broader security policies including responses to Russia.

Rising perceived geopolitical risk prompts policymakers and oversight bodies to accelerate rulemaking, export vetting, and compliance enforcement targeted at AI capabilities, directly increasing regulatory scrutiny and obligations on developers.

A spike in perceived geopolitical risk triggers a rapid risk-off reallocation and flight-to-safety, diverting portfolio and bank flows away from exposed jurisdictions into safe-haven currencies and assets, lowering net cross-border inflows to risky markets.

A rise in perceived US–China geopolitical risk drives rapid repositioning by traders and hedgers and increases speculative flows and risk premia in energy markets, producing larger and more frequent price swings.

A rising perception of acute US–China geopolitical risk reallocates diplomatic attention and some military planning among Western actors, creating short-term windows of reduced deterrence that Russia can exploit to increase kinetic and hybrid coercive actions in Ukraine.

Higher policy rates raise the cost of borrowing and compress venture/private valuations, causing banks and VC funds to pull back new financing into AI startups and projects, reducing net capital flowing into AI development.

A rise in policy interest rates raises domestic borrowing and refinancing costs for upstream producers and service contractors, delaying maintenance and new field investment and thereby reducing near‑term crude output availability.

Rising policy rates increase governments' borrowing costs and debt‑service burdens, tightening near‑term fiscal space and political willingness to approve new or sustained outlays for foreign military assistance.

Rising policy interest rates increase borrowing costs and required returns for corporate overseas projects and make home-market assets more attractive, causing firms and investors to scale back or delay outbound FDI and cross-border deals.

An upward shift in the nominal yield curve increases financing and collateral costs for inventory and hedging, destabilising storage economics and futures positions and producing larger, more frequent swings in energy prices.

A sustained upward shift in the nominal yield curve raises long‑term borrowing costs unevenly across allied economies, producing asymmetric fiscal pressures and timetables that generate political disagreements and reduce operational synchronization within coalitions.

A marked rise in nominal yields (higher curve level) raises sovereign and corporate funding stress and market volatility, which market participants interpret as heightened economic fragility and elevate perceived geopolitical risk between major powers.

Shifts by large investors toward equities and technology-heavy allocations lift public and private tech valuations and cash access for AI firms, enabling faster hiring, integration and rollout of trained models into production systems.

A tilt by institutional investors away from equities toward bonds/cash reduces availability and raises the cost of long-horizon equity and project finance, prompting delays, downsizing or cancellations of capital-intensive fab expansions and slowing near-term growth in operable capacity.

A drop in cross‑border capital flows (risk‑off/global repricing) directly reduces foreign portfolio, VC and FDI into major AI hubs, lowering the net rate of new investment available for AI development and commercialisation.

An increase in cross‑border capital flows improves access to foreign financing, spare parts and offshore contractor services for exporters and refiners, sustaining production and exports and thus raising immediate crude availability.

Higher cross‑border capital and banking flows ease financing, payment and logistics for procurement and transfers (including spare parts and munitions), directly increasing the rate and volume of defense aid that can be delivered to Ukraine.

An increase in net cross-border capital flows raises available liquidity and financing for M&A, greenfield projects and portfolio-backed expansions, directly boosting measured cross-border investment volumes.

A sustained inflow of new capital into AI-driven investment raises domestic demand, wages in high‑growth sectors and near‑term inflation expectations, prompting central banks to tighten policy rates to counter rising inflationary pressure.

A surge in domestic AI investment raises asset valuations and reduces the incentive for outbound M&A and greenfield investment abroad (and makes foreign targets more expensive), thereby lowering cross-border investment flows between blocs.

Accelerated development of novel AI capabilities produces fieldable military-relevant systems and countermeasures that external partners procure and transfer as defense assistance to preserve battlefield parity.

Rapid deployment of AI-enabled autonomous surface, subsurface and aerial systems (commercial and military) increases the number and sophistication of actor-capable platforms in choke points, raising the frequency of harassment, misidentification incidents, and attacks on shipping.

Faster operational deployment of AI-enabled systems (autonomous ISR, loitering munitions, targeting aids) increases actors' ability and lowers marginal cost of conducting cross-border or hybrid kinetic actions, raising the intensity and frequency of coercive operations.

Rapid operational deployment of advanced models in sensitive military or dual-use systems prompts regulatory bodies to impose or tighten export restrictions on those deployed model classes and related tooling.

A spike in high-profile AI safety/security incidents drives immediate re‑risking as investors sell technology and growth equities and reallocate toward bonds and cash to avoid regulatory, litigation and operational losses.

A rise in AI-related safety incidents (e.g., algorithmic trading errors, false signals, data poisoning) produces sudden, large orders and misinformation cascades in commodity markets, driving short-term spikes and greater volatility in energy prices.

High-profile AI-related incidents (autonomous-weapon malfunctions, AI-driven cyberattacks on infrastructure) that can be attributed to conflict actors prompt rapid punitive responses, including expanded multilateral sanctions and export controls.

High-profile AI safety or misuse incidents that are attributed to actors in the other country (or that cross borders) raise market and policymaker perceptions of threat and instability, increasing measured geopolitical risk between the US and China.

Tighter AI-specific rules, export controls and foreign-investment screenings directly block or delay cross-border M&A, VC funding and portfolio investment into affected firms and jurisdictions, reducing net capital movements.

Heightened AI safety and dual‑use regulation prompts governments to extend export controls and intelligence-driven compliance checks to AI-relevant transfers, increasing the operational rigor and scope of sanctions and trade enforcement targeting actors in the region.

New or intensified AI safety regulations create legal authorities and technical definitions that governments can immediately use to classify models/tools as controlled items, prompting stricter export licensing and denial criteria.

Crude oil supply availability
nodes.description: The aggregate volume of crude oil available to global markets for immediate production, export and refining.

nodes.label: Refined fuel supply availability
nodes.description: The aggregate quantity of refined petroleum products (diesel, jet fuel, gasoline) available in markets and distribution networks.

nodes.label: Maritime transit volume
nodes.description: The flow rate (number and cargo volume) of commercial vessels transiting key sea lanes per unit time.

nodes.label: Shipping and freight rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level for maritime freight and tanker chartering that influences transport costs.

nodes.label: Tanker fleet operational capacity
nodes.description: The available number and carrying capacity of tankers that are operational and deployable for crude and product transport.

nodes.label: Refinery operational capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate processing capacity of refining facilities that is online and able to produce refined products.

nodes.label: Pipeline flow rate
nodes.description: The volume per unit time of hydrocarbons transported through major pipeline corridors.

nodes.label: Energy market price volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude and frequency of price fluctuations in energy commodity markets (crude, products, LNG).

nodes.label: Spare oil production capacity
nodes.description: The amount of producible hydrocarbon output that can be brought online within a short timeframe beyond current production.

nodes.label: Military attack frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which hostile kinetic or missile/drone strikes occur against energy, shipping, or transport infrastructure.

nodes.label: Maritime security threat intensity
nodes.description: The perceived and observable level of security risk to vessels and crews in key sea lanes and chokepoints.

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement intensity
nodes.description: The strictness and operational rigor of trade, financial and transport restrictions applied to target flows and actors.

nodes.label: Trade rerouting rate
nodes.description: The pace at which commercial cargo and energy shipments are diverted to alternative routes, modes, or corridors.

nodes.label: Fuel inventory levels
nodes.description: The combined strategic and commercial stockpiles of refined fuels held in storage across markets.

nodes.label: Central bank policy response intensity
nodes.description: The magnitude and speed of monetary policy actions taken in response to energy-driven inflation and market stress.

nodes.label: Investor risk perception
nodes.description: The aggregate market sentiment reflecting investors' perceived geopolitical and market risk, as expressed in asset allocation and risk premia.

Coercive escalation intensity
nodes.description: Measures the overall rate and intensity of coercive actions (kinetic, paramilitary and hybrid operations) directed across borders and critical infrastructure.

nodes.label: Control over foreign assets
nodes.description: Measures the degree to which domestic authorities exercise de facto control or takeover of foreign‑owned assets and operations within a jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Sanctions and trade pressure
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate severity and multilaterally coordinated intensity of punitive economic measures, tariffs and trade restrictions.

nodes.label: Defense assistance flow
nodes.description: Measures the rate and volume of military aid, equipment transfers and logistical support crossing borders to conflict‑affected actors.

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the level of political and operational alignment among cooperating external actors on security, economic and diplomatic responses.

nodes.label: Corporate exposure to contested markets
nodes.description: Measures the scale and concentration of multinational commercial and operational exposure to contested or high‑risk jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Information and narrative influence
nodes.description: Measures the strength and reach of information operations, propaganda and competing narratives across media and social networks.

nodes.label: Perceived electoral legitimacy
nodes.description: Measures public and external perceptions of the credibility and acceptability of electoral processes and outcomes.

nodes.label: Energy flow stability
nodes.description: Measures the continuity, reliability and volatility of cross‑border energy supplies and related infrastructure operations.

nodes.label: Supply chain resilience
nodes.description: Measures the capacity of transnational supply chains to absorb, reroute or recover from disruptions originating in geopolitical conflict.

nodes.label: Militarisation pace
nodes.description: Measures the tempo of military build‑up, procurement and force posture changes across relevant actors and regions.

nodes.label: Cyber and network attack rate
nodes.description: Measures the frequency and intensity of cyber intrusions, disruptions and digital sabotage targeting state and civilian systems.

nodes.label: Legislative and tariff authority intensity
nodes.description: Measures the scope and assertiveness of enacted domestic legal powers, emergency statutes and tariff authorities used in economic coercion or defence.

nodes.label: Cross‑border capital and asset flows
nodes.description: Measures the volume and directionality of capital movements, investments and asset transfers between jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Domestic political stability
nodes.description: Measures the degree of social and institutional stability, protest pressure and regime resilience within affected societies.

nodes.label: Defensive military capability
nodes.description: Measures the operational readiness, integrated air/missile defence capacity and combat support capabilities available for defence.

Semiconductor fabrication capacity
nodes.description: Aggregate installed and operable advanced semiconductor fabrication capacity measured in wafer starts or equivalent production throughput.

nodes.label: Memory chip fabrication capacity
nodes.description: Total production capacity dedicated to memory (NAND/DRAM) manufacturing measured in wafers or gigabytes-equivalent output.

nodes.label: AI hardware demand rate
nodes.description: Rate of demand growth for specialized AI accelerators and related hardware measured as change in procurement or shipments per unit time.

nodes.label: Critical materials supply concentration
nodes.description: Degree to which extraction, processing and export of critical minerals and rare-earth elements are concentrated among limited suppliers or regions.

nodes.label: Supply-chain geographic diversity
nodes.description: Distributional spread of key suppliers and production nodes across different countries or regions, indicating diversification level.

nodes.label: Cross-border investment flows
nodes.description: Volume and direction of investment flows (FDI, greenfield, mergers) between economic blocs and alternative destinations per unit time.

nodes.label: Technology transfer and licensing rate
nodes.description: Rate at which advanced know-how, patents and licensing agreements move across borders or between firms measured per period.

nodes.label: Export control strictness
nodes.description: Degree of legal and administrative restrictiveness applied to outbound transfer of specified technologies, components and tooling.

nodes.label: Market access barrier level
nodes.description: Intensity of tariffs, licensing conditions, quotas and administrative hurdles that limit foreign firms' access to a given market.

nodes.label: Regulatory cooperation and alignment
nodes.description: Degree of harmonization or formal cooperation in regulatory standards and licensing regimes between relevant jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Corporate lobbying pressure
nodes.description: Intensity of private-sector advocacy efforts aimed at shaping trade, investment and technology policy outcomes measured by activity and influence.

nodes.label: Strategic stockpiles of critical inputs
nodes.description: Quantities of reserve inventories of critical minerals, components or finished tech products held for strategic or security purposes.

nodes.label: Fabrication construction and capital cost
nodes.description: Realized and expected capital expenditure per unit capacity for building semiconductor and memory production facilities.

nodes.label: Supply-chain resilience
nodes.description: System-level ability of technology supply chains to absorb, adapt to and recover from shocks measured by recovery time and redundancy.

nodes.label: Perceived geopolitical risk
nodes.description: Market and policymaker perception of geopolitical tension and conflict risk that influences strategic decisions and risk premia.

nodes.label: Alternative destination attractiveness
nodes.description: Relative attractiveness of non-primary locations for investment and production based on cost, policy incentives and supply-chain fit.

Policy interest rate
nodes.description: The short-term nominal interest rate set as the operative target of monetary policy that anchors short-term funding rates.

nodes.label: Monetary-policy communication tone
nodes.description: The hawkishness or dovishness and clarity of forward guidance and public commentary from monetary authorities as perceived by markets.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market and household expectations of future inflation over short and medium horizons.

nodes.label: Nominal yield curve level
nodes.description: The pattern of observed nominal interest rates across maturities for sovereign debt, summarising term structure pricing.

nodes.label: Real yield level
nodes.description: Inflation-adjusted yields across key maturities that capture the real return available to investors.

nodes.label: Term premium level
nodes.description: The additional yield investors demand for holding longer-duration debt beyond expected short rates.

nodes.label: Credit spread level
nodes.description: The average premium required for non-sovereign credit over comparable sovereign yields, reflecting default and liquidity risk.

nodes.label: Mortgage borrowing costs
nodes.description: The effective interest rates and lending conditions faced by home borrowers for typical mortgage products.

nodes.label: Housing market demand
nodes.description: Aggregate demand for housing transactions and purchases, including buyer activity and willingness to pay.

nodes.label: Equity risk premium
nodes.description: The excess return investors require to hold equities over risk-free assets, reflecting valuation and expected returns.

nodes.label: Asset allocation tilt
nodes.description: The distribution of investor portfolios across major asset classes (bonds, equities, cash) and shifts in that allocation.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flow rate
nodes.description: The net rate of financial capital moving between jurisdictions, including portfolio, bank and direct flows.

nodes.label: Exchange rate level
nodes.description: The relative price of a currency against relevant peers, capturing appreciation or depreciation pressure.

nodes.label: Market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease, depth and cost of executing large transactions across financial markets without large price impact.

nodes.label: Market volatility level
nodes.description: The magnitude of short- to medium-term price fluctuations and implied volatility across asset classes.

nodes.label: Systemic leverage
nodes.description: Aggregate leverage in the financial system including borrowing by intermediaries and leveraged investors.

Capital flow rate
nodes.description: The net rate at which new financial resources are invested into development, deployment, and commercialisation of advanced AI capabilities.

nodes.label: Compute capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate available high-performance compute resources (e.g., GPUs, accelerators, datacenter cycles) usable for training and running AI models.

nodes.label: AI talent supply
nodes.description: The size and skill-level distribution of the workforce qualified to build, operate, and evaluate advanced AI systems.

nodes.label: Model development velocity
nodes.description: The speed at which new model architectures, capabilities, and iterations are researched, trained, and validated.

nodes.label: Model deployment rate
nodes.description: The rate at which trained models are integrated into production systems and released into operational use.

nodes.label: Safety incident frequency
nodes.description: The occurrence rate of safety, security, or harmful-behaviour incidents attributable to deployed AI systems.

nodes.label: Safety investment level
nodes.description: The cumulative resources (funding, staff time, tools) allocated specifically to AI safety, security, and evaluation activities.

nodes.label: Regulatory pressure
nodes.description: The intensity of rulemaking, oversight, enforcement actions, and compliance expectations aimed at AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Public trust in AI
nodes.description: The aggregate level of confidence among users, voters, and the general public in AI systems' safety, reliability, and social alignment.

nodes.label: Market valuation pressure
nodes.description: The degree to which capital markets and valuation expectations create incentives to prioritise rapid growth, monetisation, or scaling of AI offerings.

nodes.label: Competition intensity
nodes.description: The strength of competitive dynamics among actors to capture market share, capabilities, and first-mover advantages in AI.

nodes.label: Independent evaluation coverage
nodes.description: The proportion of AI models and systems subjected to third-party, external safety testing, audits, or red-team evaluations.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity exposure
nodes.description: The system-level vulnerability to adversarial compromise, data exfiltration, or malicious use enabled by AI-related assets and interfaces.

nodes.label: Compute infrastructure buildout rate
nodes.description: The pace at which new datacenter capacity, specialized hardware, and supporting infrastructure are brought online for AI workloads.

nodes.label: Cross-border policy alignment
nodes.description: The degree of coordination and convergence among jurisdictions on norms, standards, and enforcement approaches for AI governance.

nodes.label: Workforce reskilling rate
nodes.description: The rate at which incumbent workers are retrained or upskilled to adapt to AI-driven changes in job tasks and labour demand.

Corporate moves to diversify supply chains away from China create new production and transshipment points, which directly increases the rate at which energy and goods shipments are re-routed to alternative sea lanes, hubs and logistics corridors.

When Western governments and firms materially diversify supply chains away from China, the reduced economic exposure lowers political risk of Chinese retaliation and makes governments more willing to impose or tighten coordinated trade and financial sanctions on Russia.

Higher cross-border investment flows inject direct equity, M&A proceeds, and venture funding into foreign AI firms and labs, immediately increasing the net rate of financial resources available for advanced AI development.

Stricter export controls block or delay shipment of high-end AI accelerators, pre-trained models, and cloud services to targeted firms, directly reducing available training throughput and slowing iteration cycles.

Tightening export controls immediately blocks transactions and raises compliance/legal risk, prompting foreign investors, banks and trading partners to pause or withdraw capital and trade finance to affected firms and jurisdictions, reducing net cross-border capital flows.

Tighter export controls on critical technologies to China prompt Beijing to accelerate spot purchases and build strategic reserves of Middle East crude to hedge against supply-chain pressure, drawing down volumes available to third‑party buyers.

Tighter export controls on advanced technologies toward China require and incentivize multilateral coordination (sharing rules, enforcement, intelligence), which increases political and operational alignment among US partners and allies on broader security policies including responses to Russia.

Rising perceived geopolitical risk prompts policymakers and oversight bodies to accelerate rulemaking, export vetting, and compliance enforcement targeted at AI capabilities, directly increasing regulatory scrutiny and obligations on developers.

A spike in perceived geopolitical risk triggers a rapid risk-off reallocation and flight-to-safety, diverting portfolio and bank flows away from exposed jurisdictions into safe-haven currencies and assets, lowering net cross-border inflows to risky markets.

A rise in perceived US–China geopolitical risk drives rapid repositioning by traders and hedgers and increases speculative flows and risk premia in energy markets, producing larger and more frequent price swings.

A rising perception of acute US–China geopolitical risk reallocates diplomatic attention and some military planning among Western actors, creating short-term windows of reduced deterrence that Russia can exploit to increase kinetic and hybrid coercive actions in Ukraine.

Higher policy rates raise the cost of borrowing and compress venture/private valuations, causing banks and VC funds to pull back new financing into AI startups and projects, reducing net capital flowing into AI development.

A rise in policy interest rates raises domestic borrowing and refinancing costs for upstream producers and service contractors, delaying maintenance and new field investment and thereby reducing near‑term crude output availability.

Rising policy rates increase governments' borrowing costs and debt‑service burdens, tightening near‑term fiscal space and political willingness to approve new or sustained outlays for foreign military assistance.

Rising policy interest rates increase borrowing costs and required returns for corporate overseas projects and make home-market assets more attractive, causing firms and investors to scale back or delay outbound FDI and cross-border deals.

An upward shift in the nominal yield curve increases financing and collateral costs for inventory and hedging, destabilising storage economics and futures positions and producing larger, more frequent swings in energy prices.

A sustained upward shift in the nominal yield curve raises long‑term borrowing costs unevenly across allied economies, producing asymmetric fiscal pressures and timetables that generate political disagreements and reduce operational synchronization within coalitions.

A marked rise in nominal yields (higher curve level) raises sovereign and corporate funding stress and market volatility, which market participants interpret as heightened economic fragility and elevate perceived geopolitical risk between major powers.

Shifts by large investors toward equities and technology-heavy allocations lift public and private tech valuations and cash access for AI firms, enabling faster hiring, integration and rollout of trained models into production systems.

A tilt by institutional investors away from equities toward bonds/cash reduces availability and raises the cost of long-horizon equity and project finance, prompting delays, downsizing or cancellations of capital-intensive fab expansions and slowing near-term growth in operable capacity.

A drop in cross‑border capital flows (risk‑off/global repricing) directly reduces foreign portfolio, VC and FDI into major AI hubs, lowering the net rate of new investment available for AI development and commercialisation.

An increase in cross‑border capital flows improves access to foreign financing, spare parts and offshore contractor services for exporters and refiners, sustaining production and exports and thus raising immediate crude availability.

Higher cross‑border capital and banking flows ease financing, payment and logistics for procurement and transfers (including spare parts and munitions), directly increasing the rate and volume of defense aid that can be delivered to Ukraine.

An increase in net cross-border capital flows raises available liquidity and financing for M&A, greenfield projects and portfolio-backed expansions, directly boosting measured cross-border investment volumes.

A sustained inflow of new capital into AI-driven investment raises domestic demand, wages in high‑growth sectors and near‑term inflation expectations, prompting central banks to tighten policy rates to counter rising inflationary pressure.

A surge in domestic AI investment raises asset valuations and reduces the incentive for outbound M&A and greenfield investment abroad (and makes foreign targets more expensive), thereby lowering cross-border investment flows between blocs.

Accelerated development of novel AI capabilities produces fieldable military-relevant systems and countermeasures that external partners procure and transfer as defense assistance to preserve battlefield parity.

Rapid deployment of AI-enabled autonomous surface, subsurface and aerial systems (commercial and military) increases the number and sophistication of actor-capable platforms in choke points, raising the frequency of harassment, misidentification incidents, and attacks on shipping.

Faster operational deployment of AI-enabled systems (autonomous ISR, loitering munitions, targeting aids) increases actors' ability and lowers marginal cost of conducting cross-border or hybrid kinetic actions, raising the intensity and frequency of coercive operations.

Rapid operational deployment of advanced models in sensitive military or dual-use systems prompts regulatory bodies to impose or tighten export restrictions on those deployed model classes and related tooling.

A spike in high-profile AI safety/security incidents drives immediate re‑risking as investors sell technology and growth equities and reallocate toward bonds and cash to avoid regulatory, litigation and operational losses.

A rise in AI-related safety incidents (e.g., algorithmic trading errors, false signals, data poisoning) produces sudden, large orders and misinformation cascades in commodity markets, driving short-term spikes and greater volatility in energy prices.

High-profile AI-related incidents (autonomous-weapon malfunctions, AI-driven cyberattacks on infrastructure) that can be attributed to conflict actors prompt rapid punitive responses, including expanded multilateral sanctions and export controls.

High-profile AI safety or misuse incidents that are attributed to actors in the other country (or that cross borders) raise market and policymaker perceptions of threat and instability, increasing measured geopolitical risk between the US and China.

Tighter AI-specific rules, export controls and foreign-investment screenings directly block or delay cross-border M&A, VC funding and portfolio investment into affected firms and jurisdictions, reducing net capital movements.

Heightened AI safety and dual‑use regulation prompts governments to extend export controls and intelligence-driven compliance checks to AI-relevant transfers, increasing the operational rigor and scope of sanctions and trade enforcement targeting actors in the region.

New or intensified AI safety regulations create legal authorities and technical definitions that governments can immediately use to classify models/tools as controlled items, prompting stricter export licensing and denial criteria.
